title_en: Swearing by the Spirits and Addressing Them
body_ar:
موضوع عمت به البلوى وهو القسم على الروحاني هل يجوز، وهل هناك روحانيون مكلفون بخدمات لحجاب؟؟

الجواب أن الروحانية المقصود به الأرواح عموما ولا يحل القسم عليها ولا خطابها لكنها موجودة فالأرواح لا تعدم ومنها أرواح شريرة وارواح طيبة فالأرواح الطيبة أرواح أهل الإيمان والتقوى والأرواح الشريرة أرواح أهل الحسد والخبث والكفر والنفاق، وهي تشمل الإنس والجن فكل له أرواح، لكن لا يقسم عليها ولا تخاطب.
body_en:
A matter with which affliction has become general: swearing by the spirit-being — is it permissible? And are there spirit-beings charged with services for the l-ḥjāb??

The answer is that by 'the spiritual' are meant spirits in general. It is not lawful to swear by them, nor to address them. But they do exist: spirits are not non-existent. Among them are evil spirits and good spirits. The good spirits are the spirits of the people of faith and God-consciousness, and the evil spirits are the spirits of the people of envy, malice, disbelief and hypocrisy. They include both humankind and the jinn, for each has spirits. But they are not sworn by and they are not addressed.

flags.arabic: وهل هناك روحانيون مكلفون بخدمات لحجاب؟؟
flags.context: the second half of the question, set against the answer
options: render faithfully and mark that the second question is not answered
read the answer as denying that such spirit-beings exist
read the answer as confirming that they exist
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. Two questions are asked and only the first is answered. The Sheikh rules on swearing by spirits and addressing them; he says nothing at all about whether there are spirit-beings assigned to serve amulets. What he does say — that spirits exist and are not non-existent — sits close enough to the unanswered question that a reader will take it for an answer to it. It is not. Nothing has been supplied in either direction.

flags.context: the questioner's term, and the Sheikh's gloss of it
options: spirit-being / the spiritual, keeping the Sheikh's own reduction of it to 'spirits in general'
flags.note: The questioner is using rūḥānī in its local, technical sense: the spirit-agents that practitioners of the amulet crafts claim to command. The Sheikh does not accept that framing — he redefines the word to mean spirits in general (al-arwāḥ ʿumūman) and answers on that basis. The English must keep both levels visible, the questioner's term and the Sheikh's reduction of it, or the answer will read as a non sequitur. 'Spiritualism' in option 2 would import a nineteenth-century European movement that has nothing to do with this.

flags.arabic: ولا يحل القسم عليها ولا خطابها
options: it is not lawful to swear by them, nor to address them
it is forbidden (ḥarām) to swear by them or address them
swearing by them and addressing them are not allowed
flags.note: The Sheikh says lā yaḥillu, 'it is not lawful', which is his own formulation, and he repeats it in the closing clause as a flat passive ('they are not sworn by and they are not addressed'). He does not use the word ḥarām and it has not been supplied, though the force of lā yaḥillu is close to it.

options: taking an oath upon the spirit-being
flags.note: al-qasam ʿalā in this context is not simply swearing an oath by something; it is adjuring a spirit — putting it under oath to compel it to act, which is what the practitioners do. 'Adjuring' captures that and 'swearing by' does not, but 'swearing by' is the more literal rendering of the Arabic and is what has been used in the body. A reviewer should decide; the distinction changes what exactly the Sheikh has ruled against.

translator_notes: The date carried here is the CMS record date. Across this whole slice the site serves a bulk-upload timestamp of 19-23 December 2010, which is when the written archive was loaded into the site, not when the Sheikh gave the answer. date_is_cms_upload is set true. The real date of composition is not recoverable from the page and has not been guessed.

'l-ḥjāb' in the question is the same Hassaniya dialect term treated at length in record 586 of this slice, where it is flagged for a fixed rendering. The same rendering must be applied to both records.

'A matter with which affliction has become general' renders ʿammat bihi al-balwā, a fixed juristic formula for a practice so widespread that it bears on the ruling. It is the questioner's phrase, not the Sheikh's.
The Sheikh gives no scriptural evidence and no citation anywhere in this record, and none has been supplied.
